prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current approaches to 3D gaze estimation face two primary bottlenecks. First, reliance on dense feature analysis (processing large pixel regions) makes models computationally expensive and highly sensitive to local noise artifacts, such as light spots, glints, and blurs common in near-eye infrared imagery. Second, the representation of the eye is typically entangled; the neural network struggles to differentiate between the intrinsic, static geometry of the eyeball (radius, center position) and the dynamic, extrinsic gaze direction (iris/pupil rotation). This coupling increases learning difficulty, as the model must simultaneously infer anatomical consistency and motion without explicit structural separation.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve robust, lightweight, and accurate 3D gaze estimation by introducing a **deformable and decoupled** learning framework. Specifically, we posit that:
1.  **Sparsity via Geometry:** By using a learnable 3D eyeball model to project semantic edges (pupil/iris boundaries) onto the 2D image, we can guide the attention mechanism to focus *only* on geometrically salient regions, thereby ignoring background noise.
2.  **Latent Decoupling:** Explicitly separating the latent space into "invariant" features (anatomy) and "variable" features (gaze/motion) will resolve the optimization conflict between short-term gaze shifts and long-term structural consistency.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose to build a model-aware network that iteratively refines a parametric 3D eye model. The architecture will function as follows:

**1. Parametric 3D Eyeball Modeling**
We will define a fully differentiable 3D eye model. Rather than treating the eye as a generic object, we will parameterize it with specific geometric properties:
*   **Invariant Parameters:** Eyeball radius, iris radius, and the 3D center of the eyeball (relative to the camera).
*   **Variable Parameters:** Pupil radius (dilation), eyeball rotation (gaze direction), and translation.
This model will serve as the core "guide" for our feature extraction.

**2. Spatial Decoupling Network (SD-Net)**
We will implement a dual-branch decoding architecture to disentangle the feature space:
*   **The Invariant Branch:** Queries and refines features related to the static structure of the eye.
*   **The Variable Branch:** Queries and refines features related to the dynamic movement of the pupil and iris.
By processing these independently but optimizing them jointly, the network learns to distinguish between a change in gaze and a change in eye shape.

**3. Deformable Sparse Attention (DSA) Mechanism**
Instead of applying global attention across the entire feature map, we will introduce a geometry-guided attention module.
*   **Projection-Based Sampling:** At each iteration, the current estimated 3D eye model is projected onto the 2D image plane.
*   **Sparse Alignment:** We identify key semantic landmarks (specifically the edges of the pupil and iris) from this projection.
*   **Deformable Attention:** The network will generate sampling points specifically around these projected edges. This effectively acts as a hard filter, forcing the network to attend *only* to the relevant anatomical boundaries and ignore noise like specular reflections on the cornea or skin texture.

**4. Iterative Refinement Loop**
The system will operate in a recursive loop. The decoupled network predicts parameters; these parameters update the 3D model; the 3D model projects new sampling points to the 2D image; and the attention mechanism uses these new points to extract cleaner features for the next refinement step. This allows the model to "lock on" to the true gaze direction end-to-end.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** We aim to establish a method for integrating explicit 3D geometric constraints into the attention mechanism of a neural network, moving beyond "black box" feature extraction to "model-aware" learning.
*   **Robustness & Efficiency:** By restricting computation to sparse, geometrically meaningful points, we expect to significantly reduce computational complexity while simultaneously improving resilience to image noise and varying lighting conditions.
*   **Disentangled Representation:** The proposed decoupling strategy will provide a more interpretible latent space, offering separate control over anatomical calibration and gaze tracking.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We utilized the TEyeD dataset and a specific architectural configuration to evaluate the De²Gaze method. The details of the setup were as follows:

*   **Dataset:**
    *   **Name:** TEyeD (The largest image dataset in the world, shot by seven different head-mounted eye trackers).
    *   **Composition:** Over 20 million images from 132 participants. Includes 2D and 3D feature points, semantic segmentation, 3D eyeball annotation, gaze vectors, and eye movement types.
    *   **Training Split:** Approximately 348,000 images randomly selected from a subset of 16 participants.
    *   **Testing Split (Subset A / Within-Subject):** Approximately 36,000 images from the same 16 participants used for training.
    *   **Testing Split (Subset B / Cross-Subject):** Approximately 16,000 images randomly selected from 12 *different* participants to verify cross-subject capability.
    *   **Preprocessing:** Temporal downsampling applied to reduce frame rate from 25Hz to 6.25Hz to ensure significant eye movements between frames.
    *   **Augmentation:** Applied 1.0-2.0 standard deviation ambiguity, 0-30% random noise, and horizontal flip of the eye image with 20% probability.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **3D Gaze Error:** Measured in degrees (°).
    *   **2D Gaze Error:** Measured in degrees (°).
    *   **Semantic Segmentation:** Intersection over Union (IoU) in percentage (%).
    *   **2D Eye Center Error:** Measured in pixels (px).
    *   **2D Pupil Center Error:** Measured in pixels (px).
    *   **Complexity Metrics:** Parameter count (Params in M) and Floating Point Operations (FLOPs in G).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone:** ResNet-18.
    *   **Transformer Encoder:** 3 encoder blocks, embedding dimension of 256, 8 attention heads, MLP expansion ratio of 2, no dropout.
    *   **Decoder:** Embedding dimension changed to 128.
    *   **Input:** Sequence of infrared near-eye frames.
    *   **Batch Size:** 128 (each batch contained 4 consecutive eye video frames).
    *   **Optimizer:** LAMB optimizer.
    *   **Scheduler:** Cosine learning rate scheduler with a 4-epoch warmup.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial rate of 2e-3, weight attenuation of 0.02. Gradually dropped to 2e-5 after 320k training iterations.
    *   **Templates:**
        *   Iris edge template: 26 points uniformly sampled (specific angular ranges used).
        *   Pupil edge template: 128 points uniformly sampled in the range [0, 2π].

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Convergence Analysis**
*   We observed that the De²Gaze method achieved a stable 3D gaze error significantly earlier than the purely query-based method (QueryDETR).
*   Our method exceeded the performance of the dense prediction method (TEyeD) after several epochs of training.

**Ablation and Feature Analysis**
*   **Decoupling:** Visualization of spatial attention maps showed that the invariant eyeball branch focused on stable geometric features (e.g., the eyelid region), which remained consistent from frame to frame. Conversely, the variable gaze branch focused on the pupil and iris regions, which correspond to movement and gaze shift.
*   **Single Branch vs. Dual Branch:** In the absence of the Spatial Decoupling Network (SDNet), the attention area in the single branch was observed to be less clear and unfocused compared to the decoupled branches.
*   **SPG Module:** Using random initialization for query vectors (w/o SPG Module) resulted in unstable training and poor convergence, indicating the necessity of prior semantics and position from 3D projection edge points.
*   **DSA Mechanism:** Standard cross-attention failed to effectively select important 2D feature points. The Deformable Sparse Attention (DSA) mechanism successfully focused on key spatial locations, avoiding interference from non-significant regions like light spots or blurs.

**Visual Prediction Quality**
*   The predicted gaze vectors were geometrically consistent with the eye's appearance in the frames.
*   The reconstructed 3D eyeball models, when projected onto the 2D plane, aligned accurately with the overall shape and position of the pupil and iris in the ground truth images.

**General Performance Findings**
*   Compared to the previous best method, our approach reduced gaze error by 48% when supervised only by the gaze tag.
*   When using only semantic loss, semantic Intersection over Union (IoU) improved by 1.7%.
*   We noted that while semantic supervision alone yielded accurate semantic regions, it resulted in suboptimal estimated gaze vectors and projected eyeball centers due to the ambiguity of 3D configurations presenting identical 2D semantics. Simultaneous supervision (Gaze + Semantics + Center) was required to reconstruct an excellent 3D eyeball model.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}

\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex

   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current 3D gaze estimation methodologies face two primary technical bottlenecks that hinder deployment in unconstrained environments. First, existing appearance-based methods predominantly rely on analyzing dense features (e.g., large pixel regions via standard Convolutional Neural Networks). This approach is inherently sensitive to local high-frequency noise, such as corneal light spots, blurs, and occlusions, and results in excessive computational complexity due to the processing of irrelevant background information.

Second, there exists a fundamental entanglement in the representation of the eyeball. An eyeball model possesses both time-invariant properties (radius, geometric center relative to the socket) and time-variant properties (gaze direction, pupil dilation, iris position). Existing model-based methods typically learn a coupled representation where these features are regressed simultaneously. This entanglement increases the difficulty of the learning manifold, as the network struggles to distinguish between changes in geometry versus changes in pose, leading to slow convergence and sub-optimal generalization.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **De²Gaze**, a framework for **Deformable and Decoupled** representation learning. Our core hypothesis is two-fold:
1.  **Sparsity via Geometric Prior:** By projecting a learnable 3D eyeball model onto the 2D image plane, we can generate sparse, semantically meaningful reference points (e.g., iris and pupil edges). Using these points to drive a Deformable Sparse Attention (DSA) mechanism will allow the network to sample only the relevant features, ignoring local noise and reducing computational overhead.
2.  **Spatial Decoupling:** We hypothesize that separating the latent space into two distinct streams—one for **invariant** geometric features and one for **variable** gaze features—will simplify the optimization landscape. We will achieve this via a dual-branch decoding architecture (SD-Net) that iteratively refines these parameters independently before recombining them for the final 3D reconstruction.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will design $\Phi$, a function that maps a sequence of near-eye frames $\mathcal{T} = \{I_1, \dots, I_n\}$ to a 3D eyeball model $e^m$, 3D gaze vector $e^g$, and 2D semantic segmentation $e^s$. The pipeline will consist of a backbone feature extractor, a Sampling Point Generation (SPG) module, a Deformable Sparse Attention (DSA) mechanism, and a Spatial Decoupling Network (SD-Net).

### 1. Learnable 3D Eyeball Model and Sampling Point Generation (SPG)
We will define the eyeball as a sphere with center $o_e$ and radius $r_e$. The pupil and iris will be modeled as ellipses to account for natural asymmetry. We will formally decouple the parameters into two sets:

*   **Invariant Parameters ($E_{inv}$):** Fixed across the sequence.
    $$ E_{inv} = \{ r_e, r_{i_x}, r_{i_y}, T \} $$
    Where $r_e$ is eyeball radius, $r_{i_x}, r_{i_y}$ are iris radii, and $T$ is the eyeball center translation in camera coordinates.
*   **Variable Parameters ($E_{var}$):** Frame-specific.
    $$ E_{var} = \{ r_{p_{x_n}}, r_{p_{y_n}}, R_n \} $$
    Where $r_{p_{x_n}}, r_{p_{y_n}}$ are pupil radii and $R_n$ is the frame-specific rotation matrix.

Using these parameters, we will generate discrete 3D point clouds for the pupil ($P_p^C$) and iris ($P_i^C$). For the pupil, the point generation is defined as:
$$ P_p^C = \{ (r_{p_x} \rho \cos(\theta), r_{p_y} \rho \sin(\theta), -L_p) \mid \rho \in [0,1], \theta \in [0, 2\pi] \} $$
Where $L_p = \sqrt{r_e^2 - r_i^2}$ is the distance from the eyeball center to the iris center. A similar formulation applies to the iris point cloud $P_i^C$.

To guide feature extraction, we will project these 3D points onto the 2D image plane using the camera intrinsic matrix $K$ and the extrinsic pose $[R|T]$:
$$ P^{2D} = K [R|T] P^C $$
Crucially, we will select only the projected **edge points** $P(e)$ to serve as the initial reference points for our attention mechanism, ensuring sparsity.

### 2. Deformable Sparse Attention (DSA) Mechanism
To replace dense convolution, we will implement a DSA mechanism that samples features near the projected geometric priors. For a set of reference points $P(e_n)$ derived from the 3D projection, we will learn offsets $\Delta_{hn}$ to allow the network to attend to the optimal local neighborhood.

The deformable reference points are calculated as:
$$ R_{hn} = P(e_n) + \Delta_{hn} $$
where $h$ indices the attention head. We will extract features from the 2D feature map $\mathcal{F}$ using bilinear interpolation at these locations:
$$ f_{hn} = W_h \cdot \mathrm{bilinear}(\mathcal{F}, R_{hn}) $$
where $W_h$ are learnable weights. The final attention output aggregates these features based on a query content vector $Q^{con}$ and attention weights $A_{hn}$:
$$ \mathrm{DSA}(Q^{con}, R_{hn}, \mathcal{F}) = \sum_{h=1}^{H} W_h' \sum_{n=1}^{N} A_{hn} \cdot f_{hn} $$

### 3. Spatial Decoupling Network (SD-Net)
We will construct a dual-branch decoder to process the decoupled parameters explicitly.
1.  **Query Construction:** We will initialize two groups of queries: $Q_{var}$ and $Q_{inv}$. Each query consists of a content vector ($Q^{con}$) capturing semantics and a position vector ($Q^{pos}$) capturing 3D coordinates.
2.  **Decoding:** The encoder feature map $\mathcal{F}$ will be partitioned into variable-level features $\mathcal{F}_{var}$ and instance-level features $\mathcal{F}_{inv}$.
3.  **Iterative Refinement:** The decoding process will occur over $N$ iterations. In each iteration, we update the eye parameters $E_{var}$ and $E_{inv}$ via the SPG module, which in turn updates the reference points for the DSA module.

The decoder layer operations for both branches will be defined as:
$$ Q^{con} = \mathrm{SelfAttention}(Q^{con}, Q^{pos}) $$
$$ Q^{con'} = \mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{DSA}(Q^{con}, Q^{pos}, \mathcal{F})) $$

### 4. Loss Formulation
To enable end-to-end training of the differentiable 3D model, we will minimize a composite loss function comprising three terms:

**A. Edge Point Projection Loss ($L_{edge}$):**
Measures the Euclidean distance between predicted sparse edge points and ground-truth 2D edge points:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edge}} = w_{\mathrm{projection}} \frac{1}{NK} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{edge}}} \| P_{nk}^{\mathrm{2Dedge}} - P_{n, \mathrm{argmin}_j}^{\mathrm{GT, 2Dedge}} \| $$

**B. Gaze Vector Loss ($L_{gaze}$):**
Mean square error between the predicted gaze vector $g_n$ and ground truth $g_n^{GT}$:
$$ L_{\mathrm{gaze}} = w_{\mathrm{gaze}} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \| g_n - g_n^{\mathrm{GT}} \| $$

**C. Eye Center Loss ($L_{center}$):**
Supervises the projected eyeball center in 2D:
$$ L_{\mathrm{center}}^{\mathrm{2D}} = w_{\mathrm{center}} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \| o_e^{2D, n} - o_e^{GT, 2D, n} \| $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Novelty:** This proposal introduces the first fully differentiable, spatially decoupled representation learning framework for 3D gaze estimation. By separating invariant geometry from variable pose, we align the network architecture with the physical reality of the eye.
2.  **Efficiency:** The Deformable Sparse Attention mechanism transforms the problem from processing dense pixel grids to processing a small set of geometrically guided points, significantly reducing FLOPs.
3.  **Robustness:** By explicitly leveraging 3D geometric constraints to guide 2D feature sampling, the system will be theoretically immune to local noise artifacts (light spots, blurs) that do not align with the projected eyeball model.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
